title: 1 John

stories.title: 📜 1 John 1
summaryBullets: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands — this is the Word of life. (1:1).
And this is the life that was revealed; we have seen it and testified to it, and we proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us. (1:2).
We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us. And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ. (1:3).
We write these things so that our joy may be complete. (1:4).
And this is the message we have heard from Him and announce to you: God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all. (1:5).
If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth. (1:6).
But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin. (1:7).
If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. (1:8).
If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. (1:9).
If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar, and His word is not in us. (1:10).
crossRefs: John 1:1: In the beginning was the Word.
John 17:3: Eternal life is knowing God and Jesus Christ.
Philippians 2:1-2: Complete joy in unity and fellowship.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דְּבַר חַיִּים (dəḇar ḥayyîm), Greek: λόγος τῆς ζωῆς (lógos tēs zōēs, NT), Aramaic: מֵימְרָא דְחַיֵּי (memrā d-ḥayyē)
translationNotes.note: Phrase combines 'word' (message, revelation) with 'life,' referring to the eternal life revealed in Christ.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ψηλαφάω (psēlaphaō)
translationNotes.note: Not a figure of speech. The verb means to feel or handle a solid object with the hands, and it is the word the risen Jesus uses in Luke 24:39, 'Touch Me and see', and the word for a mountain that could be touched in Hebrews 12:18. John stacks four claims of physical evidence in one sentence: heard, seen with the eyes, looked at closely, handled.

translationNotes.original: Greek: κοινωνία (koinōnia)
translationNotes.note: Ordinary commercial Greek before it was ever church language. A koinonos was a partner holding a share in a common enterprise, and Luke uses that exact word for James and John as Simon Peter's business partners in the fishing trade (Luke 5:10). English 'fellowship' suggests friendly company; the Greek means holding something jointly, with everything that implies.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ὁμολογέω (homologeō)
translationNotes.note: Built from 'same' and 'word': to say the same thing as someone else, to state a matter openly. It is public acknowledgement rather than a private feeling of regret, the same verb used for declaring allegiance out loud in Matthew 10:32 and Romans 10:9. In 1:9 it means saying about your sin what God says about it.

stories.keyTakeaway: John proclaims the Word of life heard, seen, and touched, inviting believers into fellowship with the Father and His Son Jesus Christ; the message is that God is light, so those who walk in the light have fellowship and the blood of Jesus cleanses them from all sin, and if we confess our sins He is faithful and just to forgive us.

stories.title: 🌿 1 John 2
summaryBullets: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father — Jesus Christ, the Righteous One. (2:1).
He Himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world. (2:2).
By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments. (2:3).
If anyone says, “I know Him,” but does not keep His commandments, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him. (2:4).
But if anyone keeps His word, the love of God has been truly perfected in him. By this we know that we are in Him: (2:5).
Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked. (2:6).
Beloved, I am not writing to you a new commandment, but an old one, which you have had from the beginning. This commandment is the message you have heard. (2:7).
Then again, I am also writing to you a new commandment, which is true in Him and also in you. For the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining. (2:8).
If anyone claims to be in the light but hates his brother, he is still in the darkness. (2:9).
Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him. (2:10).
But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness. He does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes. (2:11).
I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven through His name. (2:12).

I am writing to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I have written to you, children, because you know the Father. (2:13).

I have written to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one. (2:14).
Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. (2:15).
For all that is in the world — the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life — is not from the Father but from the world. (2:16).
The world is passing away, along with its desires; but whoever does the will of God remains forever. (2:17).
Children, it is the last hour; and just as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. This is how we know it is the last hour. (2:18).
They went out from us, but they did not belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us. But their departure made it clear that none of them belonged to us. (2:19).
You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth. (2:20).
I have not written to you because you lack knowledge of the truth, but because you have it, and because no lie comes from the truth. (2:21).
Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. (2:22).
Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well. (2:23).
As for you, let what you have heard from the beginning remain in you. If it does, you will also remain in the Son and in the Father. (2:24).
And this is the promise that He Himself made to us: eternal life. (2:25).
I have written these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you. (2:26).

And as for you, the anointing you received from Him remains in you, and you do not need anyone to teach you. But just as His true and genuine anointing teaches you about all things, so remain in Him as you have been taught. (2:27).
And now, little children, remain in Christ, so that when He appears, we may be confident and unashamed before Him at His coming. (2:28).
If you know that He is righteous, you also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of Him. (2:29).
crossRefs: Leviticus 19:2: Be holy, for I am holy.
John 8:12: Jesus the light of the world.
Romans 3:23-24: All sinned, justified by grace through Jesus.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַכַּפֹּרֶת (hakkappōret, mercy seat), Greek: ἱλασμός (hilasmós, NT), Aramaic: כַּפָּרָא (kappārā)
translationNotes.note: Refers to atoning sacrifice that removes sin and restores favor with God; tied to imagery of the mercy seat in the temple.

translationNotes.original: Greek: παράκλητος (paraklētos)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'one called alongside'. In Greek usage it named the man who stood beside a defendant in court to speak for him and lend him his own standing, not a hired professional but a patron. John's Gospel uses the identical word four times of the Holy Spirit, where English Bibles render it Helper, Comforter, or Advocate (John 14:16, 14:26, 15:26, 16:7).

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀντίχριστος (antichristos)
translationNotes.note: The word occurs in the Bible only in John's letters: 1 John 2:18, 2:22, 4:3, and 2 John 1:7. John treats it as a term his readers already knew, 'you have heard that the antichrist is coming', and then defines it twice himself: the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ, denying the Father and the Son (2:22), and every spirit that will not confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh (4:2-3). The prefix anti- carries both senses, against and in place of.

translationNotes.original: Greek: χρῖσμα (chrisma) - Hebrew: מָשַׁח (mashach)
translationNotes.note: Chrisma is the stuff smeared or poured on, from the verb chrio, to anoint, the same root that gives Christos, 'anointed one'. Under the law, olive oil poured on the head is what installed a man in office: Aaron as priest in Exodus 29:7, David as king in 1 Samuel 16:13. English loses the wordplay entirely, because in this one passage John sets the chrisma and the Christos against the antichristoi.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jesus Christ the Righteous One is the advocate and atoning sacrifice for the whole world, so those who know Him keep His commandments, walk as He walked, and love their brothers in the light; John warns against loving the passing world and announces the last hour with many antichrists, liars who deny that Jesus is the Christ, urging believers to let the anointing and what they heard from the beginning remain in them.

stories.title: 📜 1 John 3
summaryBullets: Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God. And that is what we are! The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know Him. (3:1).
Beloved, we are now children of God, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is. (3:2).
And everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure. (3:3).
Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well. Indeed, sin is lawlessness. (3:4).
But you know that Christ appeared to take away sins, and in Him there is no sin. (3:5).
No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning. No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him. (3:6).
Little children, let no one deceive you: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous. (3:7).
The one who practices sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the very start. This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil. (3:8).
Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin, because God’s seed abides in him; he cannot go on sinning, because he has been born of God. (3:9).
By this the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil: Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love his brother. (3:10).
This is the message you have heard from the beginning: We should love one another. (3:11).
Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did Cain slay him? Because his own deeds were evil, while those of his brother were righteous. (3:12).
So do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates you. (3:13).
We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers. The one who does not love remains in death. (3:14).
Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that eternal life does not reside in a murderer. (3:15).
By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers. (3:16).
If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him? (3:17).
Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth. (3:18).
And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence: (3:19).
Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things. (3:20).
Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God, (3:21).
and we will receive from Him whatever we ask, because we keep His commandments and do what is pleasing in His sight. (3:22).
And this is His commandment: that we should believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ, and we should love one another just as He commanded us. (3:23).
Whoever keeps His commandments remains in God, and God in him. And by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us. (3:24).
crossRefs: John 13:34: Love one another as I have loved you.
John 8:44: The devil a murderer from the beginning.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָוֶן / עַוְלָה (ʾāwen / ʿawlāh, sense), Greek: ἀνομία (anomía, NT), Aramaic: עולא (ʿawlâ)
translationNotes.note: Means deliberate violation of God’s law; used here to equate sin with rebellion against God’s standard.

translationNotes.original: Greek: σφάζω (sphazō)
translationNotes.note: The firstborn son of Adam and Eve, who killed his brother Abel in a field after God accepted Abel's offering and not his own (Genesis 4:1-16). John does not use the ordinary word for murder here. The Greek verb is sphazo, to cut the throat, the butcher's word for slaughtering a sacrificial animal, used again of the Lamb in Revelation 5:6.

translationNotes.original: Greek: τίθημι τὴν ψυχήν (tithēmi tēn psychēn)
translationNotes.note: The wording is lifted straight out of the Good Shepherd passage, where Jesus says it of Himself in John 10:11, 10:15, and 10:17-18. John then applies the same phrase, word for word, to what believers owe one another.

translationNotes.original: Greek: σπλάγχνα (splanchna)
translationNotes.note: Splanchna are the inward organs, the heart and liver and lungs. Greek and Hebrew both located strong feeling in the gut where English puts it in the heart, so the literal sense of 3:17 is 'shuts his inward parts against him'. The same word stands behind 'tender mercy' in Luke 1:78 and 'affection' in Philippians 1:8. The 'earthly possessions' of that verse is bios, a man's means of living.

stories.keyTakeaway: John contrasts children of God, who love and practice righteousness, with children of the devil, who sin and hate; believers know love by Christ laying down his life.

stories.title: 🌿 1 John 4
summaryBullets: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world. (4:1).
By this you will know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, (4:2).
and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming and which is already in the world at this time. (4:3).
You, little children, are from God and have overcome them, because greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world. (4:4).
They are of the world. That is why they speak from the world’s perspective, and the world listens to them. (4:5).
We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. That is how we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception. (4:6).
Beloved, let us love one another, because love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. (4:7).
Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love. (4:8).
This is how God’s love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him. (4:9).
And love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. (4:10).
Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. (4:11).
No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us. (4:12).
By this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit. (4:13).
And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world. (4:14).
If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God. (4:15).
And we have come to know and believe the love that God has for us. God is love; whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him. (4:16).
In this way, love has been perfected among us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment; for in this world we are just like Him. (4:17).
There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves punishment. The one who fears has not been perfected in love. (4:18).
We love because He first loved us. (4:19).
If anyone says, “I love God,” but hates his brother, he is a liar. For anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen. (4:20).
And we have this commandment from Him: Whoever loves God must love his brother as well. (4:21).
crossRefs: Romans 5:8: God shows love in Christ’s death.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַכַּפֹּרֶת (hakkappōret, mercy seat), Greek: ἱλασμός (hilasmós, NT), Aramaic: כַּפָּרָא (kappārā)
translationNotes.note: Refers to atoning sacrifice that turns aside wrath and restores favor; here Christ is the one sent in love as propitiation for sins.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַהֲבָה שְׁלֵמָה מְגָרֶשֶׁת אֶת־הַפַּחַד (ʾahăḇāh šəlēmāh məgārešet ʾeṯ-happaḥaḏ, sense), Greek: ἡ τελεία ἀγάπη ἔξω βάλλει τὸν φόβον (hē teleía agápē éxō bállei ton phóbon, NT), Aramaic: חובא גמורה מפרקת דחלא (ḥūḇā gemūrāh mep̄raqet deḥlā)
translationNotes.note: Phrase describing God’s love brought to maturity, removing fear of judgment.

translationNotes.original: Greek: δοκιμάζω (dokimazō)
translationNotes.note: The verb for assaying metal: putting silver or gold to the fire to find out whether it is genuine, the picture behind Proverbs 17:3 and behind faith tested like gold in 1 Peter 1:7. The law had already given Israel two tests for a prophet. Deuteronomy 18:21-22: if what he predicts does not happen, the LORD did not send him. Deuteronomy 13:1-5: even if his sign does come true, if he calls you after other gods he is not to be heard.

translationNotes.term: No one has ever seen God
translationNotes.original: Greek: θεὸν οὐδεὶς πώποτε τεθέαται (theon oudeis pōpote tetheatai)
translationNotes.note: John is repeating something the Old Testament states flatly. God tells Moses, 'You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live' (Exodus 33:20). The opening of John's Gospel carries the same line in nearly identical Greek (John 1:18).

stories.keyTakeaway: John teaches believers to test spirits, recognize true confession of Christ, and emphasizes that God is love, revealed in his Son, perfected in mutual love.

stories.title: 🕊️ 1 John 5
summaryBullets: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father also loves those born of Him. (5:1).
By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and keep His commandments. (5:2).
For this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments. And His commandments are not burdensome, (5:3).
because everyone born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith. (5:4).
Who then overcomes the world? Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God. (5:5).
This is the One who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ — not by water alone, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies to this, because the Spirit is the truth. (5:6).
For there are three that testify: (5:7).
the Spirit, the water, and the blood — and these three are in agreement. (5:8).
Even if we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater. For this is the testimony that God has given about His Son. (5:9).

Whoever believes in the Son of God has this testimony within him; whoever does not believe God has made Him out to be a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has given about His Son. (5:10).
And this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son. (5:11).
Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life. (5:12).
I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life. (5:13).
And this is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us. (5:14).
And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we already possess what we have asked of Him. (5:15).

If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he should ask God, who will give life to those who commit this kind of sin. There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin. (5:16).
All unrighteousness is sin, yet there is sin that does not lead to death. (5:17).
We know that anyone born of God does not keep on sinning; the One who was born of God protects him, and the evil one cannot touch him. (5:18).
We know that we are of God, and that the whole world is under the power of the evil one. (5:19).

And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know Him who is true; and we are in Him who is true — in His Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life. (5:20).
Little children, keep yourselves from idols. (5:21).
crossRefs: John 3:36: Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life.
Revelation 12:11: They overcame by the blood of the Lamb.
Jeremiah 10:11: Idols are worthless, false gods.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַיִם וָדָם (mayim wāḏām), Greek: ὕδωρ καὶ αἷμα (hýdōr kai haîma, NT), Aramaic: מיא ודמא (mayyā w-dammā)
translationNotes.note: Identifies the earthly witnesses tied to Jesus: water (likely baptism) and blood (his death), along with the Spirit testifying.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵטְא שֶׁאֵינוֹ לַמָּוֶת (ḥeṭʾ šeʾênō la-māweṯ, sense), Greek: ἁμαρτία μὴ πρὸς θάνατον (hamartía mē pros thánaton, NT), Aramaic: חובא דלא למותא (ḥūḇā d-lāʾ l-mūtā)
translationNotes.note: Differentiates between sins; some do not bring immediate, final judgment, while others (to death) signify rejection of God’s life.

translationNotes.original: Greek: τρεῖς εἰσιν οἱ μαρτυροῦντες (treis eisin hoi martyrountes)
translationNotes.note: Under the law no charge could be established on one witness; two or three were required (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus applies the rule in Matthew 18:16 and John 8:17, Paul in 2 Corinthians 13:1 and 1 Timothy 5:19. The number here is not decoration. John is presenting a case that meets the legal minimum, then says in 5:9 that God's own testimony outranks any human witness.

translationNotes.original: Greek: εἴδωλον (eidōlon)
translationNotes.note: In a Greek city this was not an abstract danger but the ordinary shape of public life. The patron deity had a temple, a festival calendar, a priesthood, and a trade in silver souvenir shrines, which is what started the riot at Ephesus over Artemis (Acts 19:23-41). Most meat in the market had been slaughtered at a temple before it reached the butcher (1 Corinthians 10:25-28). Keeping clear of idols meant stepping out of the town's economic and social life.

stories.keyTakeaway: John concludes that eternal life is in the Son, faith overcomes the world, the Spirit, water, and blood testify, and believers must avoid idols.

intro:
1 John was written by John the apostle, the son of Zebedee and the author of the Gospel of John, 2 John, 3 John, and Revelation. The letter itself does not contain Paul-style author identification, but the opening verses make John's apostolic eyewitness foundation explicit: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life... we proclaim to you" (1 John 1:1, 3). The early church unanimously attributed the letter to John the apostle; Irenaeus (c. AD 180, Against Heresies 3.16.5, 8) quotes 1 John explicitly as John's, and Polycarp of Smyrna (a personal disciple of John, c. AD 110, in his Letter to the Philippians, chapter 7) likewise quotes 1 John 4:2-3 by name. The letter was composed at Ephesus around AD 85-95, late in John's long life and during the same general period in which he produced his Gospel and his two shorter letters; some traditional commentators place 1 John just before John's exile to Patmos under Domitian (c. AD 95), where John would receive the visions of Revelation. The letter does not name a single congregation as its destination; the writing tone is more like a circular pastoral homily addressed to all the communities under John's care in the Roman province of Asia, with particular concern for confronting a specific local heresy threatening the churches. For the full biographical sketch of John the apostle (son of Zebedee and Salome, brother of James, originally a Galilean fisherman of Bethsaida, one of the inner three with Peter and his brother James, the disciple Jesus loved, recipient of Jesus' mother Mary at the cross, pillar of the Jerusalem church before relocating to Ephesus after AD 70, exiled to Patmos under Domitian, returned to Ephesus under Nerva, died peacefully in extreme old age around AD 100 as the only apostle not martyred), see the introduction to the Gospel of John or the introduction to Revelation.

The historical setting is the city of Ephesus in the closing decades of the first century AD, where John was the surviving apostle and senior pastor of the churches in the Roman province of Asia. The immediate occasion for the letter was the rise of a proto-Gnostic teaching that denied the full humanity of Jesus and severed Christian faith from Christian conduct. Two specific forms of this teaching can be identified in the letter: Docetism (from the Greek dokein, "to seem" or "to appear"), which held that Jesus only seemed to have a physical body and only seemed to suffer on the cross, since true deity could not contaminate itself with material flesh; and Cerinthianism, named after the proto-Gnostic teacher Cerinthus, an Ephesian contemporary of John (Irenaeus reports that John once fled the public baths at Ephesus rather than share space with Cerinthus, saying, "Let us flee, lest even the bath fall in, because Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is within," Against Heresies 3.3.4). Cerinthus taught that the divine "Christ" descended on the merely human Jesus at his baptism and departed before the crucifixion, so that the Christ never suffered. John's emphatic insistence on physical eyewitness ("we have seen with our eyes... we have touched with our hands," 1 John 1:1), on Christ coming "in the flesh" (1 John 4:2: "Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist"), and on Jesus' having come "by water and blood, not by the water only but by the water and the blood" (1 John 5:6, referring to his baptism and his crucifixion as both being events at which the divine Son was present) directly counters these teachings. The letter contains the only canonical New Testament uses of the word "antichrist" (Greek antichristos, "against-Christ" or "in-place-of-Christ"), at 1 John 2:18 ("you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come"), 1 John 2:22, 1 John 4:3, and 2 John 1:7; the same end-times figure is called "the man of lawlessness" in 2 Thessalonians 2:3-10 and "the beast" in Revelation 13. The Roman emperor at the time of writing was Domitian (AD 81-96), whose enforcement of emperor worship and persecution of those who refused was creating mounting external pressure on the same Asian churches.

1 John is the sixty-second book of the Christian Bible, the twenty-third book of the New Testament, and the fourth of the seven General Epistles. The letter has five chapters. The earliest surviving manuscripts include Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD); various papyrus fragments are slightly earlier but mostly partial. One textual note: the so-called "Comma Johanneum" or "Johannine Comma" (the explicit Trinitarian formula "For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one" inserted at 1 John 5:7 in the King James Version) is not present in the earliest Greek manuscripts of 1 John and appears to have entered the Latin manuscript tradition first, possibly as a marginal gloss before being incorporated into the text in the fourth or fifth century. Whether or not this particular wording is accepted as original, the doctrine of the Trinity rests on many other clear New Testament passages (the baptism of Jesus where the Father speaks, the Son is baptized, and the Spirit descends, Matthew 3:16-17; the Great Commission's triune baptismal formula, Matthew 28:19; the apostolic benediction, 2 Corinthians 13:14; the deity of Christ in Colossians 1:15-20, Hebrews 1:8, John 1:1, Titus 2:13, 2 Peter 1:1; and many others). Several passages in 1 John itself have become foundational to Christian theology and assurance: 1 John 1:9 ("If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness"); 1 John 3:1 ("See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are"); 1 John 4:8 and 4:16 ("God is love"); 1 John 4:19 ("We love because he first loved us"); and the assurance verse 1 John 5:13 ("I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life").
